# In Praise of the Wrong Train

## I. The Platform That Wasn’t on the Map

The mistake began with a sign.

Not an obvious mistake, not the kind accompanied by lightning bolts or red exclamation marks. The sign was small, white, and mounted between two other signs, and for several seconds I read it with the serene confidence of a person who believed he knew where he was going. The sign said Alder. I was going to Veyre.

I had been in Veyre before. Twice, years apart, and both visits had followed the same reliable pattern: arrive at the central station, take a tram marked with a yellow circle, sit beside a window while the tram navigated streets I had begun to recognize, and meet someone at a café whose name I could never remember afterward. This time the purpose was less romantic. A friend and I had arranged to meet at four in the afternoon, inspect a stack of books in an upstairs room above a restaurant, and spend the evening talking until the restaurant gradually emptied around us.

I had printed the route, copied the address into my phone, and charged my battery overnight. Everything, including the phrase everything in order, had seemed reassuring.

The train I wanted was on Platform Six. The sign for Platform Six had apparently moved.

I walked the length of the station, passing a coffee machine dispensing something dark enough to qualify as weather, a station cat asleep beneath a departures board, and a man holding a paper cup upside down while explaining to his telephone that he was, in fact, standing directly beneath the correct sign. I found Platform Three, then Platform Four, then returned to the concourse and read the board again. Veyre was due in eleven minutes. According to the little digital arrows, the platform was concealed somewhere behind vending machines and a locked door.

At 7:14, a train arrived without announcement.

Its destination was displayed in letters too dim to read. I looked at my ticket. Then I looked at the train. Then I looked at my phone, which had lost its signal and, apparently, its confidence in me.

The doors opened. An announcement said, “All passengers for Veyre, connect at the next station.” I have never learned whether this was true. I have never learned whether anyone tried to board the train because of that announcement. I only know that when the doors closed, I was sitting inside with my bag on my knees and my carefully arranged day falling quietly into a ravine.

There was no great panic. At first, there was mostly embarrassment. I had made a novice’s error in a city where I was supposed to be an occasional local authority. Then the train gathered speed, and the station roof tilted away, and I saw a porter lift a newspaper high above his head like a man waving off a rescue boat.

The carriages were half empty. A family sat together near the back. An elderly woman read a book with a cracked green cover. Two students shared a single earbud, each taking turns looking out of opposite windows. The conductor, when I showed him my ticket, shrugged in a way that suggested long familiarity with human error.

“You can get off at Arden,” he said. “It’s forty minutes. After that, we go somewhere else.”

“Can I come back?”

He looked at the timetable as if it had personally offended him. “Eventually,” he said.

Eventually, I discovered, is one of the vaguer promises a railway can make.

The city vanished. Apartment blocks gave way to warehouses, warehouses to gardens, gardens to fields divided by fences and bright strips of wildflowers. I had spent so much of the day trusting signs that I found it strangely difficult to look at the landscape without searching for an explanation. That was the station. That was the road to Veyre. That white shape was probably a hill.

I put the map away and watched the fields instead.

## II. A Hotel Without a Name

Alder had a station, a bakery, three taxis, and a street that seemed to lead nowhere except to more streets. I bought a ticket onward without knowing where it would stop. The conductor punched it and told me the return service left at 7:32 that evening, which meant I had an entire day in a town I had chosen by accident.

I found the hotel by following the smell of coffee uphill.

Its sign said Rooms, then the number twelve, though only six windows were visible from the street. The woman at the desk had gray hair pinned with a wooden spoon and an expression suggesting that questions about maps were among the more disappointing things a person could ask before breakfast.

“No maps?” she said, when I placed mine on the counter.

“Of course there are maps. There just aren’t any maps of places I can reach.”

She gave me the critical look.

“I don’t have one,” I admitted.

She examined my map upside down. “That may be for the best. This street isn’t where it used to be. The clock in the square is wrong. The fountain is where the tree is, or the tree is where the fountain was. People have opinions about it.”

She produced a pencil and drew a map on the back of an invoice. Her lines were uncertain but lively. The river leaned to the left. The road out of town became a dotted line, then stopped. She marked the bakery with a cross, the hotel with two circles, and a distant hill with a symbol I did not recognize.

“Where does this lead?” I asked, pointing to the hill.

“Depends on whether you want the long way or the old way.”

“And which is better?”

“The long way has better views. The old way has fewer steps.”

This was not an answer in the usual sense, but I wrote it down.

Room 8 overlooked a courtyard containing three bicycles, a bathtub filled with rain, and a lemon tree leaning cheerfully toward a drain. The clock on the wall had no numbers. Its hands advanced and retreated according to a principle known only to itself. There was a bowl of biscuits on the windowsill; a handwritten sign said one each, though the biscuits did not appear to have been counted recently.

I washed my face, changed shirts, and realized that I no longer had anywhere I was required to be.

There is a difference between losing something and losing track of what you are supposed to be doing. The first is a loss. The second is sometimes a postponement. I sat on the edge of the bed and looked at the clock, which appeared to believe it was still morning.

Outside, the town went about its business.

I could hear knives chopping onions, a radio playing from a window, and someone arguing cheerfully with a ladder. A delivery van double-parked below. A cat crossed the courtyard, inspected the bathtub, and declined to make a decision. None of this was urgent. None of it had been included in my itinerary.

I put the map in my pocket, but I did not unfold it.

The hotel woman’s advice had already begun to alter the day. It was not guidance, exactly. It lacked the clean authority of an arrow. It was more like a rumor passed along a fence: go by the yellow wall, but perhaps not after the construction; the bridge is open, but ask someone; if you smell bread, you are probably close.

By noon I was hungry enough to follow the smell.

## III. The Limits of Useful Advice

The bakery occupied the corner of a road that my map insisted was straight. In fact, it bent around a small square where a fountain stood in a pool of brown leaves. A boy was feedingducks from a paper bag. A dog watched the bread through the window with religious devotion.

I ordered coffee and a cheese pastry. The woman behind the counter placed them on a plate with a napkin folded into a shape that suggested experience but not enthusiasm.

“How long do I have?” I asked.

“For the coffee? If you don’t drink it, eventually.”

“I mean the town.”

She looked toward the door, as if considering the town itself. “It depends.”

“Everybody keeps saying that.”

“Usually they’re right.”

I ate on a bench in the square. The pastry was excellent, though it produced crumbs with the determination of escaped prisoners. Across the street, a tailor’s shop displayed a blue curtain in the window. Under the curtain hung a sign saying alterations, repairs, and patience. I could see no patient customers, but the word seemed to be doing most of the work.

I followed the woman’s pencil map toward a supposed shortcut. The route passed a post office, a vacant lot, a wall painted with a smiling sun, and a row of houses that ended abruptly at a construction barrier. Behind the barrier was a field. Behind the field was a hill. Behind the hill, if she had not lied, was the road to whatever came next.

A man standing beside the barrier told me the path through the field was not public.

“Public, private, or dangerous?”

He considered this. “Mostly muddy.”

I thanked him and walked around.

The hill was worth the detour. From the top, Alder appeared smaller but more complete. I could see the roofs, the river, the yard where a train waited beneath a long canopy. The pencil map had shown only a smudge where the hill should have been. Maps are often most obedient at the scale where they were drawn. They encourage us to trust the tiny blue line, not the mountains concealed beneath it.

A dog came scrambling up the path, followed by an old man carrying a cane and a plastic bag filled with apples. He stopped when he saw me looking down at the town.

“First time?” he asked.

Apparently my expression had published an article.

“Yes,” I said.

“Where are you going?”

“Veyre.”

He looked at my map in my hand. “By that map, you’re already there.”

“So I’ve heard.”

He laughed. “Then you’d better have a ticket.”

I told him I had one. He nodded as if this were a considerably better plan.

“The bridge by the station floods,” he said. “Not dangerously. Just enough to make you regret wearing the shoes you have on.”

Above us, a cloud moved across the sun, and the town became briefly metallic. Windows flashed. The river showed a pale strip of sky. Then the light returned, and the buildings looked less like objects than piles of accumulated decisions.

The old man handed me an apple from his bag. It was small and sweet and slightly bruised on one side.

“For the journey,” he said.

I asked whether the town had changed much.

“Everything changes,” he said. “The difficulty is deciding what you want to call change.”

He said this without solemnity, then went downhill, tapping his cane against stones.

I remained on the hill until the wind grew cold. The day had become larger than I expected. It no longer seemed like a delay between two points. It had its own weather, its own errands, its own unnecessary risks. There was a muddy field beside me because I had gone around the construction barrier. There was an apple in my pocket because an old man had decided I looked like someone who needed an apple.

I ate half of it and put the other half beside a stone, in case the journey required more provisions.

## IV. The Map in the Margins

I returned to the square and discovered that the map had been less helpful than advertised. The fountain was indeed where the tree was supposed to be, but the tree had vanished, apparently without consulting the authorities. A temporary sign directed pedestrians through an alley. A delivery truck blocked the road beside the bakery. I walked the wrong way twice, not because I was suddenly committed to uncertainty, but because the town had declined to cooperate with the drawing.

At the far end of the street, I found a bookshop.

The sign above the door said Books, Maps, and Other Sentences. A narrow staircase led upstairs. On the first landing, a handwritten notice instructed visitors not to discuss the price of the downstairs books. The second floor was divided between shelves, tables, cardboard boxes, and a window seat holding three cats and a pile of paperbacks.

The bookseller sat behind a desk with a cup balanced on a stack of atlases. She was reading a book about bridges. The title was Bridge: A Social History, which seemed more ambitious than the book itself.

“I’m sorry,” I said. “I’m looking for a map.”

“We have many maps.”

“I’m looking for a map of this town.”

“We have one of that, too. It may be inaccurate.”

“I’m beginning to understand that maps here have a difficult professional life.”

She smiled. “The town was rebuilt several times. The maps kept arriving too late.”

She brought out a large plan from a drawer. It was dated 1968. The river was blue, the roads red, and the buildings gray. A railway line ran through the bottom of the page, while a tram route crossed the town in a way I could not reconcile with the present. The old fountain appeared near a street that no longer existed. A factory occupied the space now occupied by a grocery store, a school, and a small dog park.

I leaned over the map.

“You might find this useful,” the bookseller said.

“It’s completely wrong.”

“Most maps are wrong about something important.”

“It was painted over.”

I looked at her.

I did not know who had written it. I bought the postcard because I believed I would understand it later, which is one of the more hopeful ways of buying things.

But the day had also contained the apple, the fountain, the cats, the hill, the bookseller’s story about ink. It had contained a bench where a stranger had pointed toward the river and a hotel owner who had turned an invoice into a map. The mistake was real. Its consequences were real. But the day was larger than the mistake.

I wrote on the postcard:

Then I added:

I did not send the postcard.

I tucked it into the book I had not yet finished, between the chapters on ordinary time and the possibility of taking the long way home.

## V. Coming Back with More Than You Left

The road back to the station seemed shorter than the road away from it. This is often the case with unfamiliar places. Arrival presents every surface for inspection; departure allows the mind to edit. The yellow wall became a blue café. The vacant lot became a parking garage. The hill disappeared behind a row of houses, and I felt a small, unreasonable grief that it could do this so easily.

I passed the construction barrier, where the muddy path was now marked by a puddle. I passed the tailor’s shop, where the blue curtain had been replaced by a red one. The sign still said alterations, repairs, and patience.

At the station, the clock said 7:26.

The return train was due at 7:32. Six minutes were enough to restore a person to the status of punctual, but not, apparently, to restore the person he had been before the morning.

I sat on the platform and took out the pencil map.

The hotel woman’s lines had blurred slightly where my hand had been damp. The river leaned more than it had when she drew it. The hill was now a nearly illegible smudge. I had added a cross beside the bakery and a small circle beside the bookshop. Near the bottom, in handwriting I did not recognize as my own, someone had written **take the long way**.

I could not remember writing it.

The phone found a signal. Several messages appeared at once: my friend asking where I was, the restaurant confirming the table, a reminder to return a book, a weather alert that did not seem urgent until I read it twice. The day had not been merely inconvenient. It had left a small collection of practical consequences behind.

I typed to my friend:

**I’m at the station in Arden. I got on the wrong train this morning. I’m sorry I missed the afternoon.**

The reply came before I had put the phone away.

**Okay. Call me when you’re back.**

I looked at the words for a while. They were not a punishment. They were not an embrace, either. They were an ordinary message, carrying the ordinary mercy of someone willing to continue a conversation after a delay.

I called. There was a moment of static, then my friend’s voice.

“Were you lost?” they asked.

“Yes,” I said.

“Was it terrible?”

I considered the hill, the apple, the fountain, the map with the missing bridge. “No,” I said, surprised. “Mostly it was just different.”

“Different how?”

I did not have a good answer. I had expected the day to reveal something. A lesson. A sudden freedom from obligation. A new and improved personality. Instead, I had returned with damp shoes, a half-eaten apple, and a postcard addressed to no one.

“It’s still Veyre,” I said. “The station is the same. Everything is where I left it.”

“That sounds disappointing.”

“It does.”

“Still, you sound different.”

“Because I got lost?”

“Because you stopped explaining.”

The train arrived with a low mechanical sigh. I told my friend I would call again after dinner. They said, “Do that.” The line went quiet.

On the train, the conductor punched my ticket in a place I did not expect. I folded the map and put it beside the window. Outside, fields gave way to houses, and houses gathered into streets. Veyre assembled itself along the tracks, familiar roofs and small platforms, the yellow circle of the tram, the route I had planned before the mistake erased the plan.

I had learned nothing that could be written as a rule. I had simply allowed an hour of my life to become unavailable to the person who had arranged it, and discovered that the world had not ended in my absence. It had continued without my supervision.

I still used maps. I still wanted to know where I was going. I still believed in arriving, in making plans, in checking the platform and charging the battery and keeping the address in my pocket. But I no longer confused knowing the route with knowing the journey. A map could tell me where a road went. It could not tell me why I was walking, what the weather meant, or whether a man with an apple would remember my face.

I kept the pencil map. I did not keep the lesson.

For once, that seemed like enough.

It made the day sound like a sequence of failures, as if the entire landscape had been assembled to expose my inadequate sense of direction.

It had contained a bench where a stranger had pointed toward the river and a hotel owner who had turned an invoice into a map. The mistake was real. Its consequences were real. The road back to the station seemed shorter than the road away from it. This is often the case with unfamiliar places. Arrival presents every surface for inspection; departure allows the mind to edit. The yellow wall became a blue café. The vacant lot became a parking garage. The hill disappeared behind a row of houses, and I felt a small, unreasonable grief that it could do this so easily.

I passed the construction barrier, where the muddy path was now marked by a puddle. I passed the tailor’s shop, where the blue curtain had been replaced by a red one. The sign still said alterations, repairs, and patience.

At the station, the clock said 7:26.

The return train was due at 7:32. Six minutes were enough to restore a person to the status of punctual, but not, apparently, to restore the person he had been before the morning.

I sat on the platform and took out the pencil map.

The hotel woman’s lines had blurred slightly where my hand had been damp. The river leaned more than it had when she drew it. The hill was now a nearly illegible smudge. I had added a cross beside the bakery and a small circle beside the bookshop. Near the bottom, in handwriting I did not recognize as my own, someone had written **take the long way**.

I could not remember writing it.

The phone found a signal. Several messages appeared at once: my friend asking where I was, the restaurant confirming the table, a reminder to return a book, a weather alert that did not seem urgent until I read it twice. The day had not been merely inconvenient. It had left a small collection of practical consequences behind.

I typed to my friend:

**I’m at the station in Arden. I got on the wrong train this morning. I’m sorry I missed the afternoon.**

The reply came before I had put the phone away.

**Okay. Call me when you’re back.**

I looked at the words for a while. They were not a punishment. They were not an embrace, either. They were an ordinary message, carrying the ordinary mercy of someone willing to continue a conversation after a delay.

I called. There was a moment of static, then my friend’s voice.

“Were you lost?” they asked.

“Yes,” I said.

“Was it terrible?”

I considered the hill, the apple, the fountain, the map with the missing bridge. “No,” I said, surprised. “Mostly it was just different.”

“Different how?”

I did not have a good answer. I had expected the day to reveal something. A lesson. A sudden freedom from obligation. A new and improved personality. Instead, I had returned with damp shoes, a half-eaten apple, and a postcard addressed to no one.

“It’s still Veyre,” I said. “The station is the same. Everything is where I left it.”

“That sounds disappointing.”

“It does.”

“Still, you sound different.”

“Because I got lost?”

“Because you stopped explaining.”

The train arrived with a low mechanical sigh. I told my friend I would call again after dinner. They said, “Do that.” The line went quiet.

On the train, the conductor punched my ticket in a place I did not expect. I folded the map and put it beside the window. Outside, fields gave way to houses, and houses gathered into streets. Veyre assembled itself along the tracks, familiar roofs and small platforms, the yellow circle of the tram, the route I had planned before the mistake erased the plan.

I had learned nothing that could be written as a rule. I had simply allowed an hour of my life to become unavailable to the person who had arranged it, and discovered that the world had not ended in my absence. It had continued without my supervision.

I still used maps. I still wanted to know where I was going. I still believed in arriving, in making plans, in checking the platform and charging the battery and keeping the address in my pocket. But I no longer confused knowing the route with knowing the journey. A map could tell me where a road went. It could not tell me why I was walking, what the weather meant, or whether a man with an apple would remember my face.

I kept the pencil map. I did not keep the lesson.

For once, that seemed like enough.
